# Spring Boot Web Application using Container Image Hygiene Checks

This runbook uses the same Spring Boot quote application as the other Spring
Boot examples, but the focus is the container image rather than Java runtime
packaging. The problem is that a Dockerfile can produce a working image while
still hiding important engineering decisions: which base image bytes were used,
which user starts the process, which command the runtime executes, which
components are packaged, and which known vulnerabilities apply to the final
artefact.

The goal is to make those decisions visible and reviewable:

Container image hygiene is not one single action. It is a set of small,
reviewable decisions that work together: reduce unnecessary privileges, make
build inputs repeatable, expose what is packaged in the image, and compare the
result with current vulnerability data. Some of these decisions reduce attack
surface, some reduce the chance of accidental drift, and some give reviewers
better evidence. None of them is enough on its own.

- what changed between a convenient baseline image and a stricter image;
- whether the application runs as root or as an unprivileged numeric user;
- how to make the startup command predictable;
- how to resolve the base image digest for repeatable builds;
- how to produce an SBOM and run a vulnerability scan when the scanning tool
  is available.

If these checks are ignored, teams ship artefacts that are harder to reproduce,
harder to explain in review, and harder to investigate during an incident. This
is not a claim that a single scan makes an image safe. Scanner results depend on
vulnerability databases, base image metadata, and the point in time when the
scan is run. Treat the output as evidence to review, not as a production
security guarantee.

This focused example does not cover every aspect of running Java in containers.
See the [all-in-one Spring Boot example](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md)
for a more holistic example that combines the workshop techniques.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the declared and effective runtime user for two images built from the
  same Spring Boot JAR;
- explain how `ENTRYPOINT`, `CMD`, and a pinned base-image digest shape a
  reviewable image contract;
- generate an SBOM and scan the built image archive for known vulnerabilities;
  and
- explain why these checks provide evidence rather than a production-security
  guarantee.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

  The commands in this runbook use Docker syntax by default. On a Podman-only
  machine, replace `docker` with `podman` for the normal `build`, `run`, and
  `image inspect` commands. The base-image digest lookup uses `crane`, so it
  does not depend on Docker Buildx.

- `jq`, used to inspect JSON output.

- [Syft](https://github.com/anchore/syft), used to generate an SBOM.

- [Trivy](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy), used to scan the image.

- [Crane](https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/tree/main/cmd/crane),
  used to inspect remote container image digests without requiring Docker
  Buildx.

- Optional: [Dive](https://github.com/wagoodman/dive), or a similar tool, for
  inspecting image layers.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The same executable Spring Boot JAR is the controlled input for each image in
this runbook. The baseline Dockerfile copies that JAR and inherits the
base-image runtime user; the non-root Dockerfile copies the same JAR with
explicit numeric ownership and runs it as that user. This isolates the effect of
the container configuration from the application packaging.

Inspect the two Dockerfiles before building the JAR. Later sections use the
entrypoint-and-command and pinned-digest variants to make specific image
contracts visible.

- The baseline image

  ```dockerfile
  FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
  WORKDIR "/opt/app"

  ARG JAR_FILE="./target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-*.jar"
  COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

  EXPOSE 8080

  ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  ```

- Running the application as non-root user

  ```dockerfile
  FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
  WORKDIR "/opt/app"

  ARG JAR_FILE="./target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-*.jar"
  COPY --chown=10001:0 ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

  # Use an arbitrary high numeric UID so the container does not run as root.
  USER 10001:0

  EXPOSE 8080

  ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  ```

## Build the application

The application is built once and then reused by the container image checks. The
build produces the executable JAR copied by every Dockerfile, so later image
comparisons use the same application artefact.

1. Build the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the executable JAR.

   This confirms that the packaged JAR works before the container steps add
   Dockerfiles and image layers to the picture.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   (*Optional*) Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Michael Corleone (character)",
     "id": 134,
     "quote": "Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer."
   }
   ```

3. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run the following sections from this example directory. Each one examines a
separate container image hygiene concern using the same packaged Spring Boot
JAR: explicit runtime identity, the startup contract, reproducible base-image
inputs, component inventory, and known-vulnerability evidence.

The steps are deliberately narrow. Treat their output as evidence for an image
review, not as a checklist that approves an image for production.

### Compare image defaults

The first hygiene check is to make the image’s runtime defaults visible. A
Dockerfile can look harmless while still inheriting important behaviour from its
base image, including the user that starts the process. If that user is not
declared in the application image, reviewers need to know whether the container
is relying on an inherited default or on an explicit decision made by this
Dockerfile.

This section builds two images from the same application JAR. The baseline image
keeps the base image defaults. The stricter image copies the application for,
and runs it as, a numeric non-root user. Comparing them makes the tradeoff
concrete: the application code is the same, but the runtime identity is
different.

The commands check both the declared image configuration and the effective
identity observed when a container starts. Looking at both matters because image
metadata explains what the Dockerfile requested, while `docker run` shows what
the runtime actually applies.

1. Build the baseline image.

   This step assumes the application JAR already exists in `target/`. It does
   not rebuild the Java application.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-baseline' \
     --tag 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:baseline' \
     .
   ```

2. Build the non-root image.

   This step assumes the application JAR already exists in `target/`. It does
   not rebuild the Java application.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-non-root' \
     --tag 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root' \
     .
   ```

3. Check which user each image declares.

   ```shell
   docker image inspect 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:baseline' \
     --format 'baseline user={{.Config.User}}'
   docker image inspect 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root' \
     --format 'non-root user={{.Config.User}}'
   ```

   An empty value means the image uses the base image default user. The stricter
   image declares the numeric `10001:0` user explicitly.

   ```
   baseline user=
   non-root user=10001:0
   ```

4. Compare the effective runtime identity.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm --entrypoint id 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:baseline'
   docker run --rm --entrypoint id 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root'
   ```

   The second command should show the numeric user configured by the Dockerfile.

   ```
   uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
   uid=10001(10001) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
   ```

The result is a small but useful piece of evidence. The baseline image leaves
the runtime user implicit, so reviewers have to infer the behaviour from the
inherited image configuration. The non-root image makes the decision explicit in
this Dockerfile, and the `id` command confirms that the container starts with
that identity.

This matters because the runtime user affects the blast radius of a failure. If
the application, a dependency, the JVM, or the container configuration is
abused, a process running as root has more privilege inside the container than
it needs. Running as non-root does not make the image secure by itself, but it
removes an unnecessary privilege from the default execution path.

The bigger gain is auditability. After this check, you are not saying “I think
the base image probably does the right thing.” You are saying:

- this Dockerfile declares the runtime user;
- the built image metadata contains that declaration;
- a started container actually runs with that identity.

That gives reviewers evidence instead of assumptions. It also makes later
changes easier to catch: if someone removes `USER 10001:0`, the difference is
visible in both `docker image inspect` and the `id` check.

### Image startup contract

A container image does not only package files. It also publishes a startup
contract: which executable is launched, which default arguments are supplied,
and which parts an operator can replace at `docker run`, Kubernetes, or CI time.

That contract matters because most failures are not caused by an obviously
broken Dockerfile. They happen when the image starts differently from what an
engineer, deployment manifest, or runbook assumes. A debug command may append
unexpected arguments. An environment-specific Spring profile may replace the
wrong part of the command. A production override may work in a shell example but
fail once the same image is run by an orchestrator.

`ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` are not mutually exclusive. A useful pattern for
application images is to keep the executable fixed with `ENTRYPOINT` and put
replaceable default arguments in `CMD`. That gives the image a clear default
behaviour while still allowing deployments to change configuration arguments
without replacing the Java command itself.

For example:

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY --chown=10001:0 ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

# Use an arbitrary high numeric UID so the container does not run as root.
USER 10001:0

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
CMD ["--server.port=8080"]
```

With both instructions present, the container runtime combines them. Running the
image with no extra arguments starts:

```shell
java -jar app.jar --server.port=8080
```

Passing arguments after the image name replaces `CMD`, not `ENTRYPOINT`:

```shell
docker run [IMAGE] --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

which starts:

```shell
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

The current Dockerfiles in this example intentionally do not define `CMD`. That
keeps the later `--entrypoint id` diagnostic simple. If an image defines both
`ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`, overriding the entrypoint can still append the default
`CMD` arguments to the replacement executable. That is useful to know, and it is
also why `ENTRYPOINT` should not be treated as a security boundary.

Ignoring this contract creates review and operations risk. Engineers may not
know whether they are replacing the executable or only the arguments, and a
deployment can silently stop applying the options that set ports, profiles,
memory behaviour, diagnostics, or feature flags. For a Spring Boot service, that
can mean the application starts on the wrong port, uses the wrong profile,
misses expected JVM flags, or becomes harder to debug during an incident.

The practical review question is simple: can another engineer look at the
Dockerfile and predict exactly what starts by default, what changes when extra
arguments are passed, and what happens when the entrypoint is overridden for
diagnostics? If the answer is no, the image startup contract is too implicit.

### Pin the base image

A base image tag is a dependency, not just a convenient name. When a Dockerfile
says `FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1`, the tag tells
readers the intended Java line, but it does not prove which image bytes were
used for a particular build. Registries can republish tags, and different build
machines can pull the tag at different times.

The primary reason to pin the base image is reproducibility: rebuilding the same
source commit should not silently produce a different container because a
registry tag moved. If the base image changes without a code review, a rebuild
can pick up different operating system packages, Java updates, certificates,
shell tools, or vulnerability metadata. The application code may be identical,
but the container artefact is not.

Pinning the base image with a digest makes the input explicit. The tag remains
useful for humans, while the digest identifies the exact image manifest pulled
by the build. This is not a reason to freeze images forever. It is a way to make
base image updates intentional: update the digest, rebuild, scan, test, and
review the change like any other dependency update.

Workshop examples can show tags for readability, but production build pipelines
should challenge tag-only base images unless there is a deliberate update policy
somewhere else in the build system.

1. Resolve the digest for the base image used by the Dockerfiles.

   ```shell
   crane digest 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1'
   ```

   Use the resolved digest to replace the placeholder in
   `containers/Dockerfile-pinned-digest`. This returns the manifest-list digest,
   so the pinned base image can still resolve to the correct platform image on
   both `linux/arm64` and `linux/amd64`.

   ```
   sha256:947650420cbf1a8d0ade992ed0cdc2edab4f8d4da1b80f501a56d3392e09e921
   ```

   The pinned base image reference for this platform is:

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1@sha256:947650420cbf1a8d0ade992ed0cdc2edab4f8d4da1b80f501a56d3392e09e921
   ```

2. Use this value to replace the placeholder in
   `containers/Dockerfile-pinned-digest`.

   ```dockerfile
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1@sha256:947650420cbf1a8d0ade992ed0cdc2edab4f8d4da1b80f501a56d3392e09e921
   WORKDIR "/opt/app"

   ARG JAR_FILE="./target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-*.jar"
   COPY --chown=10001:0 ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

   # Use an arbitrary high numeric UID so the container does not run as root.
   USER 10001:0

   EXPOSE 8080

   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
   ```

The important point is not that this specific digest is permanently better than
the tag. The point is that the Dockerfile now records the base image as a
reviewable input. If a future build should use a newer Java image, the digest
change becomes visible in version control, the resulting image can be scanned
again, and reviewers can discuss the update as a dependency change instead of
discovering it after a rebuild behaves differently.

### Generate an SBOM

After the image is built, the next question is simple: what is actually in it? A
Spring Boot container includes more than application classes. It also includes
the Java runtime, operating system packages from the base image, nested
dependency JARs, launch scripts, certificates, and any tooling copied into the
image along the way.

An SBOM records that inventory in a machine-readable format. It does not prove
that the image is safe, and it does not replace source review, patching, or
runtime hardening. Its value is evidence: engineers and automation can inspect
the components that were present in the artefact that was actually built.

Without an SBOM, reviews often fall back to weaker questions such as “what did
the Dockerfile probably copy?” or “which dependencies does Maven list?” Those
are useful inputs, but they are not the same as an inventory of the final
container image. If a vulnerability, licence question, or incident appears
later, the team needs a concrete component list to search and compare.

1. Build the image.

   This step assumes the application JAR already exists in `target/`. It does
   not rebuild the Java application.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-non-root' \
     --tag 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root' \
     .
   ```

2. Save the image as a local archive for scanner input.

   Passing an explicit archive to scanners keeps the workflow tied to the image
   built in the current Docker context instead of relying on each tool to
   discover the image by tag.

   ```shell
   docker save \
     --output 'target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar' \
     'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root'
   ```

3. Generate the SBOM from the saved image archive.

   ```shell
   syft 'docker-archive:target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar' \
     --output 'cyclonedx-json=target/sbom.cdx.json'
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the generated Software Bill of Materials for the
   container image was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -P 'sbom.cdx.json' --prune './target'
   ```

   The Software Bill of Materials in CycloneDX JSON format.

   ```
   ./target
   └── sbom.cdx.json

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

4. (*Optional*) View the summary from the Software Bill of Materials.

   ```shell
   jq '.metadata.component.name, (.components | length)' 'target/sbom.cdx.json'
   ```

   This prints the image archive described by the SBOM and the number of
   discovered components.

   ```
   "target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar"
   8737
   ```

The useful review artefact is `target/sbom.cdx.json`, not the short summary
printed by `jq`. Keep the SBOM tied to the image that was built and scanned,
because the inventory only has meaning when it describes a specific artefact. In
a real pipeline, this file would usually be stored with the build output or
attached to the image provenance so later reviews can answer “was this component
present?” without rebuilding from assumptions.

### Scan the image

Vulnerability scanning answers a different question from the previous checks: do
the packages and libraries in this built image match known vulnerability data?
That is why scanning is intentionally last. First make the image contents,
runtime identity, base image input, and SBOM explicit, then scan the artefact
that those decisions produced.

This ordering matters. If a scan reports a critical issue, engineers need to
know which image was scanned, which base image it came from, which components
were present, and whether the process runs with unnecessary privileges. If a
scan is clean, the same context prevents a false sense of security. Scanner
output depends on vulnerability databases, package metadata, scanner rules,
severity mappings, and the time when the scan runs.

Ignoring scanning leaves teams blind to known issues in code they did not write:
operating system packages, Java dependencies, and tooling inherited from the
base image. Treating scanning as the only security check creates the opposite
problem. A scan can miss misconfiguration, excessive privileges, weak update
practices, or vulnerabilities that have not been published yet.

1. Build the image to scan.

   This step assumes the application JAR already exists in `target/`. It does
   not rebuild the Java application.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile-non-root' \
     --tag 'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root' \
     .
   ```

2. Save the image as a local archive for scanner input.

   Scanning the archive keeps this step tied to the image built above instead of
   relying on a scanner-specific lookup by tag.

   ```shell
   rm -rf 'target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar'
   docker save \
     --output 'target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar' \
     'container-image-hygiene-spring-boot:non-root'
   ```

3. Scan the saved image archive.

   ```shell
   trivy image \
     --severity HIGH,CRITICAL \
     --ignore-unfixed \
     --input 'target/container-image-hygiene-spring-boot-non-root.tar'
   ```

   Review scanner findings in context. A clean scan is not a substitute for
   provenance, patching, image pinning, and runtime hardening.

The useful outcome is not the word “passed” or “failed”. The useful outcome is a
reviewable finding list tied to a specific image artefact. For each finding,
decide whether the fix belongs in the application dependency tree, the base
image, the Dockerfile, or the deployment policy. Also record when a finding is
accepted temporarily, because vulnerability data changes and yesterday’s
acceptable risk can become today’s release blocker.

- [Syft](https://github.com/anchore/syft)
- [Trivy](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- A working image can still hide important runtime defaults; inspecting image
  metadata and the effective process identity makes the runtime-user decision
  reviewable.
- `ENTRYPOINT`, `CMD`, and a pinned base-image digest turn startup behaviour and
  build inputs into explicit contracts, but they require disciplined update and
  review practices.
- An SBOM records what was present in a specific built image, and a
  vulnerability scan compares that inventory with current data; neither proves
  that an image is safe for production.
- Image hygiene reduces hidden assumptions and improves incident evidence, but
  deployment policy, patch management, and runtime hardening remain separate
  engineering decisions.
